articleSummary: Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and COVID-19 are contrasted amid renewed Ebola concerns. Ebola spreads mainly through direct contact with infected body fluids or contaminated surfaces, with outbreaks historically in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda. COVID-19 spreads primarily through airborne droplets and aerosols, enabling spread. Symptoms differ: Ebola causes high fever, severe weakness, vomiting, diarrhea, and possible internal or external bleeding; COVID-19 causes fever, cough, sore throat, shortness of breath, fatigue, and loss of smell or taste. Fatality rates for Ebola have ranged roughly 25%–90% depending on strain and care; COVID-19 fatalities are lower but higher in total cases. Treatments: early use of Ebola regimens like Inmazeb and Ebanga with supportive care; COVID-19 relies on antivirals, oxygen, steroids, and vaccines. Vaccines exist for both; prevention includes PPE, isolation, and Ebola vaccination during outbreaks, and vaccination plus masks for COVID-19. India and others are boosting surveillance and airport screening.

articleHeadline: Can Ebola Spread Through Air? Separating Facts from Myths
articleSummary: Ebola, caused by orthoebolaviruses (formerly ebolavirus), can cause severe illness and death; first identified in 1976 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and is found primarily in sub-Saharan Africa. As outbreaks rise in parts of Africa, myths about airborne spread persist. Ebola is not classified as airborne: transmission mainly occurs through direct contact with an infected person, animal, or deceased person, via blood or other bodily fluids (saliva, vomit, urine, feces, sweat, breast milk, semen) or contaminated surfaces or medical equipment. Airborne transmission is not supported in real-world settings; virus-containing droplets exist only under highly controlled lab conditions. Mosquitoes do not spread Ebola. Early outbreaks often involve exposure to infected wildlife, particularly fruit bats. Healthcare workers protect themselves with PPE (gown, gloves, mask, face shield) to prevent exposure to fluids and potential droplets. Public education helps combat misinformation and guide prevention.

articleSummary: Canada notes: Hantavirus is nationally notifiable with about 4–5 confirmed cases annually, usually from rodents in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia; Andes strain can spread person-to-person. articleHeadline: 10 Essential Facts About Hantavirus and Ebola Virus Disease
articleSummary: Hantaviruses cause two major syndromes: HCPS in the Americas and HFRS in Old World strains. Incubation is 2–4 weeks; early symptoms are nonspecific. Transmission is mainly zoonotic from rodent excreta in rural Canada (Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia); the Andes strain has documented human-to-human transmission. Diagnosis relies on serology and PCR, with confirmation at labs such as Canada’s National Microbiology Laboratory in Winnipeg. Treatment is supportive, and Andes infections require strict airborne, droplet, and contact isolation to prevent nosocomial spread. Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreaks occur primarily in Central and West Africa, involving Zaire, Sudan, and Bundibugyo species. Bundibugyo outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo show a case-fatality of about 30–50%. Transmission is via direct contact with infected fluids; incubation ranges from 2 days to 3 weeks. Diagnosis is via real-time PCR; PPE and isolation are critical. Vaccines using recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus–based platforms target Zaire ebolavirus and have reduced mortality, while Bundibugro lacks approved vaccines or targeted therapies; care remains supportive.

articleSummary: Democratic Republic of the Congo faces a severe Ebola outbreak driven by Bundibugyo virus, a rarer Ebola strain. Existing vaccines, notably Ervebo (a vesicular stomatitis virus, VSV, vector vaccine against Zaire Ebola), do not effectively curb transmission of Bundibugyo. Ebola glycoprotein envelopes differ substantially across strains—about 35% of surface glycoproteins differ between Zaire and Bundibugyo—limiting cross-protection. Ervebo may offer some protection against Bundibugyo, but not enough to justify deployment in the current outbreak, according to experts. A 2011 primate study showed ~75% survival against Bundibugyo after Zaire-specific vaccination, yet this is not sufficient for human use in this context. WHO notes cross-immunity data are limited and inconclusive. Authorities are accelerating development of experimental vaccines, but concerns about vaccine hesitancy persist if protection is insufficient. Several candidate vaccines are on a priority development list, underscoring the need for new tools to halt transmission.

articleSummary: Published 2026-06-22, researchers from Guangdong Academy of Agricultural Sciences’ Center for Agricultural Biological Genomics Research, with Argentina’s INTA and partners, established a novel receptor–ligand interaction mediated competitive recognition paradigm to rapidly evaluate beta-coronavirus cross-species transmission risk to humans. In a China study of 70 patients with ocular symptoms, viral particles were detected inside the eye and CMNV antibodies were present in their blood. Mouse experiments produced similar eye findings, lending support to a connection. About 70% of patients reported exposure to raw or undercooked seafood; however, some had no seafood contact, suggesting other potential transmission routes. CMNV is widespread in marine species and has been detected across diverse regions, indicating a possible global risk. If confirmed, this would be the first linkage between a marine virus and human ocular disease. Preventive measures include avoiding raw seafood, washing hands after seafood contact, and seeking prompt eye examination for pain, redness, or blurred vision.

articleSummary: On 2026-06-22, Vinmec Phú Quốc treated a 92-year-old woman with pneumonia, sepsis due to Escherichia coli, leading to acute respiratory failure. Instead of invasive mechanical ventilation, clinicians used high-flow nasal oxygen, avoiding intubation. They implemented aggressive, individualized care: antibiotics for bacteremia, meticulous fluid balance, continuous cardiac and respiratory monitoring, bedside blood cultures and imaging, and early rehabilitation including chest physiotherapy and prone/positioning management every 3 hours to mobilize secretions and prevent atelectasis. A multidisciplinary 'rapid response chain' across ICU, labs, imaging, and rehabilitation enabled bedside management on the island. articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo surpasses 1,000 cases, with 1,003 confirmed and 254 deaths as of June 22, per the DRC Ministry of Health. Authorities warn the official tally may undercount due to a collapsing health system, suggesting many infections remain undetected and could surge. Reported contact tracing effectiveness is at 55% claimed by the government, but Africa CDC estimates only about 12% actual tracing, meaning most infections go untracked and continue spreading. Funeral practices involving handling of deceased bodies are a key transmission driver, with on-site funerals contributing to multiple new infections. International support has reached roughly $910 million in pledges, yet Africa CDC cautions needs could climb to $1.5 billion if the outbreak remains uncontrolled, risking a broader global health catastrophe.

articleSummary: Outbreaks of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo, hantavirus on a cruise ship, and diphtheria in Australia illustrate how distrust in health systems and poor public communication fuel infectious-disease responses. In DR Congo, at the end of May residents burned a Médecins Sans Frontières tent for suspected and confirmed Ebola cases, prompting 18 people suspected of infection to leave the treatment center. Safe-burial protocols exist since 2014 but depend on community trust; intimidation and attempts to recover bodies reflect lack of trust. The cruise-ship hantavirus outbreak underscores how misinformation thrives without clear, transparent public-health messaging; CDC visibility and international engagement were criticized in this context. In Australia, diphtheria outbreaks show that absence of information can undermine vaccination efforts, highlighting calls for transparent explanations, acknowledgment of uncertainties, frequent briefings, and diverse messengers to restore confidence.
notes: 記事はオーストラリアのジフテリア、不特定の船舶でのハンタウイルス、DRコンゴのエボラを言及しているが、対象国リストではDRコンゴのみ該当。エボラ（DRC）とジフテリア（豪州）は確認されたが、豪州は対象国外。複数の高リスク感染症が異なる地域で同時発生しており、公衆衛生コミュニケーション（不信感・ワクチン接種拒否）の失敗が共通の背景として報告されている。

articleHeadline: True scale of Congo Ebola outbreak still unknown one month in, responders say
articleSummary: Ebola virus disease is circulating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, with 782 confirmed cases and 181 deaths across Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu—already the third deadliest outbreak on record. True scale remains unknown due to data gaps and undercounting; testing remains a major weakness, with communities lacking kits and treatment centers facing lab-result delays. Data from labs, hospitals/treatment centers, and surveillance are hard to harmonize, risking under- and over-counts as patients cross zones. The virus is believed to have been circulating since February. The outbreak has reached 31 of at least 90 health zones; only 14 treatment facilities exist across nine zones, with gaps like Nizi where no facility exists, causing home deaths. Community resistance and violent incidents hinder response; a funeral was dispersed with tear gas; burial teams attacked. MSF and WHO call for strengthened diagnostics, surveillance, care access, and safe burial practices to contain the outbreak.

HFMD is caused by Coxsackie A16 and Enterovirus 71, not Singapore or seasonal influenza. Transmission occurs via droplets, saliva, feces, or vesicle fluid; children under 10 and crowded school settings are most at risk. Outbreaks peak during seasonal transition and the dry season, aided by hot, humid climates. Symptoms include fever (often >38.5°C) and vesicular rash on hands, feet, buttocks, knees/elbows, with possible mouth ulcers. Prevention emphasizes handwashing, school disinfection, personal-item separation, cough etiquette, and good nutrition/rest.

articleSummary: WHO published the first unified clinical management guidelines for filovirus diseases, covering Ebola and Marburg infections. Presented June 17 and released on 2026-06-22, the guidance integrates decades of outbreak experience to standardize care in resource-limited settings, including Democratic Republic of the Congo Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak. It applies to Ebola, Sudan, Bundibugyo, Taï Forest, and Marburg viruses, and targets clinicians and health systems worldwide. The 16 recommendations span care pathway, emphasizing systematic clinical and laboratory monitoring, early detection of deterioration, and management of reversible complications. Priorities include dehydration and shock management (early oral and IV rehydration; vasopressors for severe cases), treatment of bacterial coinfections, control of hemorrhagic manifestations, and prioritized lab tests for metabolic derangements. When vaccines or antivirals are unavailable for filoviruses, timely supportive care can markedly improve survival. The guidelines address survivor follow-up and post-discharge care and aim to strengthen preparedness, including equipment, lab capacity, drugs, and trained personnel.

articleSummary: Listeria monocytogenes biofilms persist in food processing environments, posing a food-safety threat. Lactiplantibacillus plantarum L-1, isolated from traditional Chinese Jiangshui, shows probiotic potential with 68.9% survival at pH 2.0 and 85.0% in 0.3% bile salts, and a safety profile (no γ-hemolysis, antibiotic susceptibility, no mouse toxicity). At sub-MICs (1/32–1/8 MIC) it inhibits biofilm formation in a concentration-dependent manner, reaching 89.5% at 1/4 MIC, without inhibiting planktonic growth. It reduces metabolic activity and EPS, disrupts biofilm structure, and downregulates biofilm-related genes, signaling potential as a dual-functional probiotic and natural biocontrol agent in the food industry.

articleHeadline: DR Congo's Ebola outbreak yet to peak as cases surpass 1,000
articleSummary: DR Congo’s Ebola outbreak, caused by Bundibugyo virus, has surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases and 254 deaths as of 22 June 2026. The epidemic remains active and growing, centered in eastern DRC with Bunia in Ituri province as an epicenter. Early symptoms resemble malaria and many patients lack classic bleeding signs, delaying diagnosis. So far 100 patients have recovered while 365 are in isolation or hospitalised. Authorities say the outbreak is in an ascending phase and has not peaked. Laboratory capacity has risen from about 20 tests per day to more than 2,000, and nine dedicated Ebola treatment centers have been established, with plans for more. Gaps include 58% contact-tracing versus a 95% target, and only about 12% of an estimated 35,000 contacts under follow-up. Africa CDC and WHO mobilized about $910 million; total needs could reach $1.5 billion.

articleHeadline: O papel estratégico dos hospitais nas emergências infecciosas
articleSummary: Ebola and other viral hemorrhagic fevers pose ongoing threats, though Brazil is considered at low risk for an Ebola case by health authorities. Hospitals are now strategic nodes for surveillance and containment, driven by transnational disease spread due to increased international travel. Rapid recognition of a suspected case triggers isolation, restricted circulation, strict use of personal protective equipment, and minimization of exposed staff. Preventing transmission within hospitals is critical, as failures in PPE removal, waste disposal, or hygiene can heighten risk. Continuous training, drills, and a culture of safety are integrated into high‑complexity facilities, reinforced by lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic. Brazil lists Ebola among notifiable conditions; suspicion mobilizes epidemiological surveillance, laboratory investigation, and contact tracing. Modern protocols reflect a shift from reactive responses to routine, structural preparedness for highly transmissible, deadly diseases.

articleSummary: Two deadly infections, Ebola and hantavirus, have resurfaced in public health alerts. Both diseases begin with non-specific febrile symptoms—fever, fatigue, and body aches—complicating early differentiation from other illnesses. Hantavirus transmission concentrates in rural settings with rodent exposure. The Bundibugyo Ebola variant illustrates a severe form for which there are no vaccines or specific antivirals yet; by contrast, Zaire ebolavirus has vaccines and antivirals that reduce mortality. Across these infections, infection control and mandatory reporting to health authorities remain the most reliable tools to interrupt transmission.

articleSummary: Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has reached 1,003 laboratory-confirmed cases and 254 deaths as of June 22, 2026, showing a case-fatality rate of about 25.3%. Nearly all transmissions occur in Ituri province (91.3% of infections, 80.7% of deaths), a remote northeast region. The outbreak was declared on May 15 and has also spread to neighboring Uganda, with 19 cases and 2 deaths reported. The rise in confirmed cases is partly attributed to improved testing capacity. The event is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no licensed vaccine or specific treatment. Ebola has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past fifty years.

articleSummary: Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda have led the World Health Organization to declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. Immunology experts say turning Ebola into a global pandemic like COVID-19 is unlikely due to environmental constraints in West Africa, the disease's short incubation, and the need for direct contact with body fluids for transmission. Cases are detected and isolated more easily because symptoms are severe and appear rapidly. Risk factors include weak health systems, unsafe funeral rites, cross-border travel, and delayed case-finding. Incubation is typically up to four days; bleeding and organ failure emerge in the second week, with death around day 11, though about 10% recover if the condition improves. Prevention is critical for healthcare workers, caregivers, funeral personnel, and those handling wildlife.

articleHeadline: Plague was killing children 5,500 years before the Black Death
articleSummary: 5,500-year-old plague outbreaks in hunter-gatherer camps near Lake Baikal, East Siberia, show Yersinia pestis was already deadly before agriculture and urban life. In four cemeteries, 46 individuals were analyzed; plague DNA was found in 18 (about 39%). The ancient strains carried a unique superantigen toxin, enabling highly lethal infections even without flea-rodent transmission. A high proportion of children and young teens were buried together within a short radiocarbon-dated span, indicating outbreaks in small, mobile communities. The findings challenge the view that plague's danger required dense populations and fleas. Direct transmission from marmots to humans is suggested, with outbreaks likely predating cities by millennia and supporting an origin in Central or Northeast Asia before spreading west across Eurasia. Published in Nature on 2026-06-22.
notes: 本記事は古代遺跡（シベリア、バイカル湖近辺）の考古学的分析に基づいた学術論文発表であり、現在の感染症監視対象外。Bluedot APIが「Thailand」「Russian Federation」を場所タグとして付与しているが、記事サマリーの内容は歴史的・考古学的な研究であり、現在のこれらの国での感染症アウトブレイクではない。したがってverified_locationsは空配列。

articleSummary: Ashanti Regional Health Directorate launches a mass drug administration to eliminate river blindness (onchocerciasis) and bilharziasis (schistosomiasis) in nine endemic districts: Ahafo North, Asante Mampong, Atwima Mponua, Offinso North, Ejura Sekyeredumase, Sekyere East, Sekyere Central, Sekyere Kumawu, and Sekyere Afram Plains. articleHeadline: Ebola Cases Surpass 1,000, UN Rushes Aid to DR Congo
articleSummary: As of 22 June 2026, Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo exceed 1,000, with the outbreak centered in Ituri (Mongbwalu, Rwampara, Bunia) and spreading to North Kivu and South Kivu. Roughly 130–135 orphans in Ituri are receiving support, including psychosocial care; UNICEF has opened a nursery for separated children and plans two more. Testing capacity has improved, but surveillance and contact tracing remain constrained by insecurity and clashes with armed groups. In Bunia Central Prison, 2,000 inmates benefit from a four‑bed Ebola isolation and care unit built by WHO and MONUSCO to reduce transmission and protect detainees and the wider community, highlighting prison infection prevention as a public‑health priority.

articleHeadline: How bird flu spread across the world after first detection
articleSummary: H5N1 bird flu was first detected on a goose farm in Guangdong, China, in 1996. In 1997 avian-to-human transmission occurred in Hong Kong, infecting 18 people with 6 deaths. By October 2005 the virus reached Europe, with a Turkey farm outbreak and Romania’s Danube delta flocks. Croatia reported the first wild-bird outbreak, and by December 2005 Ukraine had widespread poultry infections. By 2006 Europe faced a wild-bird–driven spread, with 13 of 24 nations reporting poultry infections. Romania endured 163 outbreaks; Russia 149; Ukraine 42 before the wave declined around 2008–2009. The last incursions were in Bavaria, Germany, and Tyva Republic. Tens of millions of wild and domestic birds died or were culled. Mammals including red foxes, otters, Arctic foxes, badgers, polecats, raccoon dogs, seals, and porpoises. Cats, dogs, and mink farms indicated mammal-to-mammal transmission. Netherlands detected antibodies in cows. WHO records 933 human cases and 477 deaths worldwide (48% CFR).

articleHeadline: Ebola en RDC : plus de 1 000 cas, à peine 1 contact sur 8 suivi
articleSummary: 1,003 confirmed Ebola cases and 254 deaths in the DRC since mid-May, as of June 21, marking the 17th outbreak. The Bundibugyo strain is involved, with Ituri as the epicenter and foci in Bunia and Mongbwalu, plus cases in North Kivu and South Kivu. There is no approved vaccine or specific treatment for this strain. Diagnosis is difficult: many patients do not bleed, and initial symptoms mimic malaria, delaying care. Surveillance expansion has driven a rapid response: more than 500 beds, over 1,000 community relays, and laboratory capacity increasing from about 20 tests per day to over 2,000; nine treatment centers are now operating. articleSummary: As of 22 June 2026, Ebola outbreak in Ituri province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, reports 1,003 confirmed cases and 254 deaths, with 100 recoveries and 365 patients hospitalized or under observation. Declared on 15 May, the outbreak may still be rising, with contact tracing coverage around 55%, hindering containment. No confirmed index case or patient zero, and more than 35,000 exposed individuals remain unlocated. The outbreak involves Bundibugyo ebolavirus, a rare variant with no specific vaccines or approved treatments, raising concern over undetected transmission. Security challenges in Ituri, including armed groups, have displaced about 2 million internally and 320,000 refugees in risk zones. The Kigonze camp in Bunia (over 20,000 residents) has reported ten unusual deaths recently, though no Ebola cases are confirmed there. WHO has issued its highest alert.
notes: 稀有なBundibugyo ebolavirus型の流行であること、ワクチンおよび承認された治療法が存在しないこと、接触者追跡カバー率が55%に留まることが懸念要因。セキュリティ課題により約200万人が国内避難民として、32万人が難民として危機にさらされている。WHOの最高警戒レベル発令は国際的な対応の必要性を示唆。

articleSummary: On June 22, Ho Chi Minh City’s Children's Hospital treated an 11-year-old boy from An Giang Province for fulminant myocarditis with cardiogenic shock. He initially had fever and vomiting, then developed dyspnea and fatigue, progressing to respiratory failure and hypotension. Local facilities required oxygen, fluids, and vasopressors before transfer. Echocardiography showed a severely reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 25–28% with elevated troponin I. PCR confirmed Rhinovirus infection (a common cold virus). He received antibiotics, transfusions, electrolyte/acid-base correction, and ultimately veno-arterial ECMO. He developed multiorgan dysfunction (liver and kidney injury) necessitating six sessions of continuous renal replacement therapy. After nearly three weeks on ECMO and about 1.5 months of care, cardiac function recovered, hemodynamics stabilized, and weaning from ECMO and ventilation was achieved; organ functions normalized. Rhinovirus is common in children and accounts for 1–5% of viral myocarditis; parents should seek medical care rather than self-medicate.

articleHeadline: Amazon land use patterns reveal where vector-borne diseases collide
articleSummary: Brazilian Amazon vector-borne disease co-occurrence is shaped by agrarian economy and socioenvironmental contexts, linking forest livelihoods, mining, poverty, and large-scale agriculture to where malaria, dengue, leishmaniasis (ATL and VL), and Chagas cluster. From 2015–2019, 1.28 million VBD cases were reported; malaria accounted for ~75%, dengue ~20%. Rural areas saw higher Chagas, malaria, and ATL; urban areas higher visceral leishmaniasis; dengue not stratified. Using a generalized linear latent variable model, researchers found Chagas and malaria co-occur, dengue and ATL co-occur, while VL tends to be isolated. Covariates explained about 75% of covariance; deforestation and rural poverty linked to urban+rural Chagas co-occurrence. Malaria-Chagas hotspots span the Western Amazon; dengue-ATL hotspots in the southeast Amazon, with 97% of dengue-ATL municipalities dominated by livestock farming/export. Agricultural land, forest fragmentation, mining, and grain production influence patterns; forest-core peasant economies correlate with higher Chagas/malaria.
notes: 本記事は学術的な疫学分析レポート（News Medical Life Sciences掲載）であり、最新のアウトブレイク報告というより、過去5年間のデータ分析に基づく地理的・社会的リスク要因の解析と推察される。アマゾン地域における複数疾患の共発生メカニズムについての研究知見であり、急性の公衆衛生上の脅威というより長期的な地域保健課題の提示と考えられる。国際的拡大やWHO通知基準は満たさず、経過観察段階が適切。

articleHeadline: A Silent Severe Myocarditis Due to Legionella Pneumophila in An Infant - Indian Journal of Pediatrics
articleSummary: 5-month-old female infant in India presented with 3 days of fever, cough, tachypnea and cyanosis, progressing to respiratory failure. Imaging showed pneumonia with echocardiography revealing EF ≈35% and biventricular dysfunction, plus moderate tricuspid and mitral regurgitation; heart structurally normal otherwise. IVIG was given for suspected viral myocarditis, but 24 hours later no improvement. Endotracheal secretions’ multiplex PCR returned positive for Legionella pneumophila. Levofloxacin was started, with marked improvement in cardiac contractility and reduced ventilator needs within 48 hours; extubation occurred at 72 hours. Discharge EF ≈45%, with progressive recovery to complete normalization at 3 months.
